summary: A 1969 network timetable, a project-schedule style memo listing tasks that needed to be done to bring a site onto the ARPANET, such as preparing facilities, obtaining specifications from the network contractor, and designing a host-to-IMP interface. It is a planning document, not a protocol.

eli5.summary: This is a to-do list with deadlines for plugging a computer into the new network, like a checklist for setting up a new classroom.

subtitle: A project schedule for connecting Stanford Research Institute to the new ARPANET.

tldr.problem: Stanford Research Institute (SRI) needed to know the steps, timeline, and dependencies for connecting their computer to the new ARPANET.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4 is a detailed project plan with dates and milestones: installing communication gear (August 1969), designing the host-IMP interface (September), testing with UCLA and other sites (October through December), and running terminal and file services.
tldr.outcome: This document is a historical record of how the ARPANET was built site by site. The milestones achieved largely on schedule.

today: RFC 4 is a historical document showing how the ARPANET was deployed in its first year. It illustrates the careful planning and staged testing used to bring a new site online.

sections.title: Overview and Phases
sections.content: RFC 4 is a work schedule from March 1969 for SRI's connection to the ARPANET. It breaks down all the tasks needed into phases with target dates: installation of communication gear by August 1, design and build the host-IMP interface by September 1, IMP installation by September 15, debug the interface by October 1, and begin testing messages with other network sites. Each phase includes detailed subtasks, responsible parties, and dependencies.
sections.eli5: This is the to-do list for the SRI team, divided into weeks and months. Each item has to be done before the next one can start.

sections.title: Installation and Testing Phases
sections.content: The early phases focus on hardware: getting specifications from BBN (the IMP contractor), coordinating with AT&T and the telephone company for circuit installation, and designing the interface between SRI's computer and the IMP (Interface Message Processor). By October, debugging begins with test messages exchanged between UCLA and SRI. Subsequent phases cover expanding to more network nodes (UCSB in November, Utah in December) and eventually running multi-user remote terminal services, file transfer, and other applications.
sections.eli5: First the team gets all the wires and hardware. Then they test by sending practice messages back and forth. Once that works, they test with other computers on the network, then turn on the mail and file services.

sections.title: Testing and Debugging Procedures
sections.content: The schedule includes detailed testing protocols: verifying message transfers in both directions, checking for message loss and duplication, testing crash and recovery procedures, and developing debugging techniques. Tests include loop-back transmission (sending data to the IMP and back), message format validation, and system response to errors and faults. The team plans to develop voice coordination between sites (telephone conference calls) to support debugging and fault isolation.
sections.eli5: The tests check that messages actually get through, that broken connections can be fixed, and that the system can handle mistakes without crashing.
